# Background
Public transit is central to sustainable urban transportation. A full train or bus carries many more people per unit of road or track space, energy and emissions than private vehicles carrying the same number of travelers, reducing traffic congestion, greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution and the land devoted to roads and parking. Transit also widens access to jobs, schools, health care and other destinations for residents who cannot drive or do not own a car, including many lower-income, older, younger and disabled residents [@toddlitman2017; @litman2014]. Rail systems such as the CTA L do this at a scale few other modes can match, and their stations help shape denser, walkable neighborhoods where walking, biking and transit together are practical alternatives to driving.

Whether people actually ride transit depends on *mode choice*: the decision, for each trip, to drive, take transit, bike, walk or not travel at all. Travelers weigh travel time (including walking to and waiting at stations), cost, reliability, safety, comfort and convenience against the alternatives available to them. These factors vary by neighborhood and by person. Residents who live near frequent rail service, who do not own a car, or whose jobs require them to be on site tend to rely more on transit, while those with cars, flexible schedules or the ability to work from home have more options. Changes in any of these factors, whether in service, fares, land use, employment or perceptions of risk, can shift travelers from one mode to another, and the effects are often uneven across communities [@litman2009].

The COVID-19 pandemic was one of the largest disruptions to mode choice in recent history. Stay-at-home orders, the shift to remote work and school, concerns about the risk of infection in crowded vehicles, and service cuts dramatically reduced transit ridership in Chicago and other cities, while some travelers shifted to driving, biking or walking. Yet not everyone could stop riding: many essential workers, often living in the communities most vulnerable to COVID-19, continued to depend on transit to reach their jobs. How quickly, and where, ridership has recovered since then has important implications for transit agency finances, service planning, equity and the region's climate and congestion goals.

This exercise examines trends in CTA L ridership between 1999 and 2026 and how the COVID-19 pandemic influenced train travel, both overall and across specific lines (e.g., Green, Pink, Red), stations and communities with different socioeconomic and health characteristics. It concludes by asking you to propose strategies for improving ridership across the city. The steps below walk you through creating the tables, maps and plots for your presentation. *As with previous exercises, combine all materials into a single presentation. Download the presentation template [via this link to the PowerPoint slides](https://justenvirons.org/pedagogy/GEO330/Exercise_03/slides/Exercise03_Template.pptx). Each slide includes placeholders for the figures and discussion questions referenced in the steps below.*

# Step 2. Compare L ridership before and after the COVID-19 pandemic
In this step you will compare CTA L ridership before, during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, first for the system as a whole by month and by day, and then for selected lines and stations. Keep in mind the factors that shape mode choice described in the background section as you interpret each figure.

## COVID-19 trends
The Chicago Data Portal provides daily COVID-19 cases and deaths, which can be plotted to identify the waves of the pandemic and compared with trends in rail ridership. Because COVID-19 is no longer a notifiable disease, local health departments such as the Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH) are no longer required to report cases to the CDC, and the city's reporting ended in May 2024.

@fig-covidcases7davg shows the 7-day average of COVID-19 deaths in Chicago. Create a custom version of the plot by changing the layer in the code below from 7-day average deaths ("Deaths7d") to 7-day average cases ("Cases7d"). *In slide 1 of your presentation, paste your custom plot of COVID-19 cases and identify the major waves of the pandemic. When were cases highest, and how did the waves differ in size and timing? Keep these waves in mind as you compare them with ridership in the slides that follow.*

```{r}
#| label: define COVID-19 plotting functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the COVID-19 plotting functions"

# L line colors; names match station_line and the rail lines' COLOR column
pal_line <- c(Blue = "#3498db", Brown = "#964B00", Green = "#1e8449", Multi = "#424949",
              Orange = "#e67e22", Pink = "#f5b7b1", Purple = "#7d3c98", Red = "#e74c3c",
              Yellow = "#f4d03f")

# function for applying the layout shared by the exercise's plots: y axis title,
# horizontal legend below the plot, unified hover labels and an image download
# button that saves the plot as filename.png
fx_plot_layout <- function(p, y_title, filename, x_title = "") {
  p %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE,
           modeBarButtons = list(list("toImage", "resetScale2d")),
           toImageButtonOptions = list(filename = filename)) %>%
    layout(
      xaxis = list(title = x_title),
      yaxis = list(title = y_title),
      legend = list(
        font = list(size = 10),
        orientation = "h",
        xanchor = "center",
        x = 0.5, y = -0.1),
      hovermode = "x unified")
}

# function for plotting COVID-19 cases or deaths by date; layer is "Cases7d" or
# "Deaths7d" (7-day averages), "Cases" or "Deaths" (daily) or "Casescm" or
# "Deathscm" (cumulative)
fx_plot_covid <- function(covid19_cases_summary, layer = "Deaths7d") {
  layer_titles <- c(Cases7d = "COVID-19 Cases (7-day average)",
                    Deaths7d = "COVID-19 Deaths (7-day average)",
                    Cases = "COVID-19 Cases",
                    Deaths = "COVID-19 Deaths",
                    Casescm = "COVID-19 Cases (cumulative)",
                    Deathscm = "COVID-19 Deaths (cumulative)")
  title <- layer_titles[[layer]]

  plot_ly(data = filter(covid19_cases_summary, layer == !!layer),
          x = ~Date,
          y = ~value,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = "#9F1928", width = 0.5),
          name = title,
          hovertemplate = paste0(title, ': %{y:,}<extra></extra>')) %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = title,
                   filename = paste0("covid19_", tolower(layer), "_chicago"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-covidcases7davg
#| fig-cap: COVID-19 Deaths (7-day average) by Day, Chicago, Illinois

fx_plot_covid(covid19_cases_summary, layer = "Deaths7d") # EDIT HERE

```

## CTA L ridership
The Regional Transportation Authority (RTA) reports on the location and performance of the three public transit operators in metropolitan Chicago: Pace Suburban Bus, the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA, both bus and rail) and Metra commuter rail. This exercise focuses on CTA rail ridership using two datasets: (1) daily rail boardings for all L stations (`ridership_daily_boardings`, from the Chicago Data Portal); and (2) monthly boardings by L station from January 1999 through `r format(ridership_through, "%B %Y")` (`ridership_attributes`, [downloaded from RTAMS](https://rtams.org/media/datasets/cta-ridership)).

```{r}
#| label: define ridership plotting functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the ridership plotting functions"

# function for plotting total boardings (all stations) by month; day_type is
# "Weekday", "Saturday" or "Sunday/Holiday"
fx_plot_ridership_by_month <- function(ridership_attributes, day_type = "Weekday") {
  ridership_by_month <- ridership_attributes %>%
    filter(day_type == !!day_type) %>%
    group_by(year_month) %>%
    summarise(rides_total = sum(rides_total), .groups = "drop")

  plot_ly(data = ridership_by_month,
          x = ~year_month,
          y = ~rides_total,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = "#080967", width = 0.5),
          name = 'Total boardings',
          hovertemplate = 'Rides: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = paste0("Total Rail Station Boardings (", day_type, ")"),
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_month")
}

# function for plotting daily rail boardings (all stations); day_type is "W"
# (weekday), "A" (Saturday) or "U" (Sunday/holiday)
fx_plot_daily_boardings <- function(ridership_daily_boardings, day_type = "W") {
  plot_ly(data = filter(ridership_daily_boardings, day_type == !!day_type),
          x = ~service_date,
          y = ~rail_boardings,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          line = list(color = "#9F1928", width = 0.5),
          name = 'Rail boardings',
          hovertemplate = 'Rail boardings: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = "Daily Rail Station Boardings",
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_day")
}
```

### Ridership by line
@fig-ridershipbyline plots weekday ridership by L line ("Multi" refers to stations served by more than one line). Review the plot and identify two lines you'd like to explore further. Create a custom plot comparing them by uncommenting the line beginning with `# a_station_line_list` and replacing the line names (e.g., replace "Blue" with "Green"). The two lines you select are also used to map changes in ridership by station below. *In slide 3 of your presentation, paste your custom plot and compare ridership on the two lines over time. How did each line's ridership change during and after the pandemic, and which has recovered more? Consider the neighborhoods and destinations each line serves (e.g., downtown, airports, universities, hospitals) and how the trips people make on each line may have changed.*

```{r}
#| label: define ridership by line plotting function
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the ridership by line plotting function"

# function for plotting weekday boardings by month and station line; lines is a
# list of line names (e.g., c("Blue", "Red")), all lines by default
fx_plot_ridership_by_line <- function(rail_stations_ridership, lines = names(pal_line)) {
  ridership_by_line <- rail_stations_ridership %>%
    filter(station_line %in% lines) %>%
    group_by(year_month, station_line) %>%
    summarise(rides_total = sum(rides_total), .groups = "drop")

  plot_ly(data = ridership_by_line,
          x = ~year_month,
          y = ~rides_total,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          color = ~station_line,
          colors = pal_line,
          text = ~station_line,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = "Total Weekday Rail Station Boardings",
                   filename = "cta_rail_boardings_by_line")
}
```

### Ridership by L station
Next, map changes in weekday ridership at stations on the two lines you selected (@fig-selectstations). Stations shown in red lost riders between `r format(ridership_through, "%B")` 2019 (before the pandemic) and `r format(ridership_through, "%B %Y")` (the latest month available), while stations shown in blue gained riders. Comparing the same month in both years keeps seasonal differences out of the comparison. Larger circles indicate larger percentage changes. Hover over a station to see its boardings in both months and its net and percentage changes. *In slide 4 of your presentation, paste your map and describe the geographic pattern of ridership change along the two lines. Which stations have recovered the most and least? Consider the land uses around each station, such as downtown offices, residential neighborhoods, universities and major destinations, and how the pandemic may have changed travel to each.*

```{r}
#| label: define station change functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the station change functions"

# function for calculating the change in weekday boardings by station between
# two months (from and to, as "YYYY-MM-DD"); to is the latest month by default and
# from is the same month in 2019 (before the pandemic) by default, so both months
# are in the same season. Only stations on the selected lines are kept.
fx_station_change <- function(ridership_attributes, rail_stations, lines = names(pal_line),
                              from = NULL, to = NULL) {
  to <- if (is.null(to)) max(ridership_attributes$year_month) else as.Date(to)
  from <- if (is.null(from)) lubridate::make_date(2019, lubridate::month(to), 1) else as.Date(from)

  ridership_attributes %>%
    filter(day_type == "Weekday", year_month %in% c(from, to)) %>%
    group_by(station_id) %>%
    summarise(rides_from = sum(rides_total[year_month == from]),
              rides_to = sum(rides_total[year_month == to]),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(net_chg = rides_to - rides_from,
           pct_chg = net_chg / rides_from * 100,
           month_from = from,
           month_to = to) %>%
    filter(is.finite(pct_chg)) %>%
    inner_join(rail_stations %>%
                 select(station_id, station_name, station_line, comarea_id, comarea_name),
               by = "station_id") %>%
    st_as_sf() %>%
    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
    filter(station_line %in% lines)
}

# function for creating the base map shared by the exercise's maps: CARTO
# basemap, reset and full screen buttons and community area boundaries for
# reference (added first, so they are drawn beneath the other layers)
fx_basemap <- function(map_data, carto_api_key = CARTO_API_KEY) {
  leaflet(data = st_transform(map_data, crs = 4326)) %>%
    addTiles(urlTemplate = paste0(
      "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/rastertiles/light_all/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=",
      carto_api_key
    )) %>%
    addResetMapButton() %>%
    addFullscreenControl() %>%
    addPolygons(
      fill = FALSE,
      color = "#555",
      weight = 1,
      opacity = 1)
}

# function for adding L lines (colored by line) and stations; lines and stations
# are drawn in their own panes, above the community areas. station_labels are the
# stations' hover labels and color is the stations' outline color; other circle
# marker options (e.g., radius, fillColor) are passed through ...
fx_add_rail_layers <- function(map, rail_lines, rail_stations, station_labels, color = "#fff", ...) {
  map %>%
    addMapPane("lines", zIndex = 440) %>%
    addMapPane("stations", zIndex = 450) %>%
    addPolylines(
      data = st_transform(rail_lines, crs = 4326),
      weight = 3,
      opacity = 1,
      color = ~unname(pal_line[COLOR]),
      options = pathOptions(pane = "lines"),
      group = "L Lines") %>%
    addCircleMarkers(
      data = st_transform(rail_stations, crs = 4326),
      color = color,
      weight = 1,
      opacity = 1,
      fillOpacity = 0.9,
      label = station_labels,
      options = pathOptions(pane = "stations"),
      group = "L Stations",
      ...)
}

# function for adding L lines and stations colored by the change in weekday
# boardings (red: loss, blue: gain; larger circles for larger percentage changes),
# with hover labels and a legend that is shown along with the stations
fx_add_station_change_layers <- function(map, station_change, rail_lines) {
  month_from <- format(station_change$month_from[1], "%b %Y")
  month_to <- format(station_change$month_to[1], "%b %Y")
  change_colors <- c(Loss = "#d7301f", Gain = "#2171b5")

  # station hover labels
  station_labels <- sprintf(
    "<strong>%s Station</strong><br/>
    <i>Line:</i> %s<br/>
    <i>Community area:</i> %s<br/>
    <i>%s weekday boardings:</i> %s<br/>
    <i>%s weekday boardings:</i> %s<br/>
    <i>Net change:</i> %s<br/>
    <i>Percent change:</i> %0.1f%%<br/>",
    station_change$station_name,
    station_change$station_line,
    station_change$comarea_name,
    month_from, format(station_change$rides_from, big.mark = ","),
    month_to, format(station_change$rides_to, big.mark = ","),
    format(station_change$net_chg, big.mark = ","),
    station_change$pct_chg) %>%
    lapply(htmltools::HTML)

  map %>%
    fx_add_rail_layers(rail_lines,
                       station_change,
                       station_labels,
                       radius = rescale(abs(station_change$pct_chg), to = c(4, 12)),
                       fillColor = unname(change_colors[if_else(station_change$pct_chg < 0, "Loss", "Gain")])) %>%
    addLegend("bottomright",
              colors = unname(change_colors),
              labels = c("Loss", "Gain"),
              title = paste0("Change in Weekday Boardings<br>", month_from, " to ", month_to),
              opacity = 0.9,
              className = "info legend circle-legend",
              group = "L Stations")
}

# function for mapping the change in boardings by station along the selected
# lines; the layer control turns the lines and stations on and off
fx_map_station_change <- function(station_change, rail_lines, community_areas_ses,
                                  lines = names(pal_line)) {
  fx_basemap(community_areas_ses) %>%
    fx_add_station_change_layers(station_change, filter(rail_lines, COLOR %in% lines)) %>%
    addLayersControl(
      overlayGroups = c("L Lines", "L Stations"),
      options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE, position = "topright"))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-selectstations
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Change in Weekday Ridership by L Station, ", format(ridership_through, "%B"), " 2019-", format(ridership_through, "%Y"))

# calculate the change in weekday boardings by station for the selected lines,
# between the latest month and the same month in 2019
ridership_attributes_station <- fx_station_change(ridership_attributes, 
                                                  rail_stations, 
                                                  lines = a_station_line_list)

# map the change in boardings by station and the selected lines
fx_map_station_change(ridership_attributes_station, 
                      rail_lines, 
                      community_areas_ses, 
                      lines = a_station_line_list)

```

# Step 3. Examine ridership by community characteristics
In this step you will examine how L ridership, and its recovery since the pandemic, varies across communities with different socioeconomic and health characteristics. The step uses the same community indicators from the [Chicago Health Atlas](https://chicagohealthatlas.org) [@chicago_healthatlas] that you explored in Exercise #2. Each indicator is stored as a column in the `community_areas_ses` table, which you loaded in Step 1.

| Column | Indicator | Health Atlas topic | Period |
|:-------|:----------|:-------------------|:-------|
| `SVI` | Social Vulnerability Index | [SVI](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/SVI) | 2022 |
| `poverty` | Poverty rate | [POV](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/POV) | 2020-2024 |
| `inactivity` | Adult physical inactivity rate | [HCSPAP](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSPAP) | 2016-2018 |
| `mortality` | All-cause mortality rate | [VRDTHR](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/VRDTHR) | 2020-2024 |
| `transit` | Ease of walking to transit stop rate | [HCSWTSP](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSWTSP) | 2023-2024 |
| `violence` | Perceived neighborhood violence rate | [HCSNVP](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSNVP) | 2023-2024 |

Follow the topic links for a full description of each indicator, including its units and data source. Before interpreting your results, note whether higher values of an indicator signal more or less advantaged conditions. For example, a higher poverty rate or Social Vulnerability Index signals less advantaged conditions, whereas a higher rate of residents who can easily walk to a transit stop signals more advantaged conditions.

## Map community indicators with L stations
@fig-mapses maps the community indicators by community area, grouped into quintiles, along with L lines and stations. Use the "Map" dropdown list in the upper right of the map to switch between indicators, and the checkboxes below it to turn L lines and stations on and off. Hover over community areas and stations for more details. Change the color palette in the code below ([see this reference for palette names](https://i0.wp.com/1.bp.blogspot.com/-3VQwNXWga9s/UICXF7rbvLI/AAAAAAAAAUg/UQBmpUO9kVA/s1600/display-brewer-all.png)) to create a custom version of the map. *Choose one indicator for the remainder of this step. In slide 5 of your presentation, paste your custom map showing that indicator and describe any visual relationship you see (or don't see) between the indicator and the location of L lines and stations. Which parts of the city have the least advantaged conditions, and how well do L lines and stations serve them? Which community areas are farthest from an L station?*

```{r}
#| label: define indicator mapping functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the indicator mapping functions"

# function for creating a quintile color palette; when repeated values make some
# quintile breaks identical, the remaining distinct breaks are used instead.
# The legend shows the range of values in each quintile.
fx_quintile_pal <- function(values, palette = "YlGn") {
  breaks <- unique(quantile(values, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2), na.rm = TRUE))
  if (length(breaks) < 2) breaks <- c(breaks, breaks + 1)
  colorBin(palette = palette, domain = values, bins = breaks, na.color = "#cccccc")
}

# function for creating community area hover labels with the value of every
# community indicator
fx_ses_labels <- function(community_areas_ses, indicators = ses_indicators) {
  values <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(indicators)), function(i) {
    sprintf("<i>%s:</i> %s<br/>",
            indicators$name[i],
            formatC(community_areas_ses[[indicators$column[i]]], format = "f",
                    digits = if (indicators$column[i] == "population") 0 else 1,
                    big.mark = ","))
  })
  values <- matrix(values, nrow = nrow(community_areas_ses))
  paste0("<strong>", community_areas_ses$comarea_name, "</strong><br/>",
         apply(values, 1, paste, collapse = "")) %>%
    lapply(htmltools::HTML)
}

# function for adding one community area layer and legend per measure, plus a
# dropdown list (top right) that shows one measure at a time; the first measure
# is shown when the map opens. measures and pals are named lists of values and
# their color palettes.
fx_add_measure_layers <- function(map, map_data, measures, pals, labels) {
  for (i in seq_along(measures)) {
    values <- measures[[i]]
    pal <- pals[[i]]
    map <- map %>%
      addPolygons(
        data = map_data,
        fillColor = pal(values),
        label = labels,
        weight = 2,
        opacity = 1,
        color = "white",
        dashArray = "3",
        fillOpacity = 0.7,
        group = names(measures)[i]) %>%
      addLegend("bottomleft",
                pal = pal,
                values = values,
                title = names(measures)[i],
                opacity = 1,
                className = paste0("info legend measure-legend measure-legend-", i - 1))
  }
  map %>%
    htmlwidgets::onRender("
      function(el, x, data) {
        var map = this;
        var groups = [].concat(data.groups);
        // show the selected measure's layer and legend and hide the others
        function show(i) {
          groups.forEach(function(g, j) {
            var layer = map.layerManager.getLayerGroup(g, false);
            if (layer) {
              if (j === i) { map.addLayer(layer); } else { map.removeLayer(layer); }
            }
          });
          el.querySelectorAll('.measure-legend').forEach(function(d) {
            d.style.display = d.classList.contains('measure-legend-' + i) ? '' : 'none';
          });
        }
        var control = L.control({position: 'topright'});
        control.onAdd = function() {
          var div = L.DomUtil.create('div', 'leaflet-bar');
          div.style.background = 'white';
          div.style.padding = '4px 6px';
          div.innerHTML = '<label style=\"font-weight: bold; margin-right: 4px;\">Map</label>';
          var select = L.DomUtil.create('select', '', div);
          groups.forEach(function(g, j) {
            var option = L.DomUtil.create('option', '', select);
            option.value = j;
            option.text = g;
          });
          select.onchange = function() { show(parseInt(select.value)); };
          L.DomEvent.disableClickPropagation(div);
          L.DomEvent.disableScrollPropagation(div);
          return div;
        };
        control.addTo(map);
        show(0);
      }", data = list(groups = names(measures)))
}

# function for mapping community indicators by community area (quintiles) with L
# lines and stations (white circles); the dropdown list switches between
# indicators and the layer control turns the lines and stations on and off.
# palette is any RColorBrewer palette name (e.g., "YlGn", "Purples", "Greys")
fx_map_ses <- function(community_areas_ses, rail_lines, rail_stations,
                       indicators = ses_indicators, palette = "YlGn") {
  map_data <- st_transform(community_areas_ses, crs = 4326)
  indicators <- filter(indicators, column != "population")

  measures <- setNames(lapply(indicators$column, function(column) map_data[[column]]),
                       paste(indicators$name, "Quintiles"))
  pals <- lapply(measures, fx_quintile_pal, palette = palette)

  # station hover labels
  station_labels <- sprintf(
    "<strong>%s Station</strong><br/>
    <i>Line:</i> %s<br/>
    <i>Community area:</i> %s",
    rail_stations$station_name,
    rail_stations$station_line,
    rail_stations$comarea_name) %>%
    lapply(htmltools::HTML)

  fx_basemap(map_data) %>%
    fx_add_measure_layers(map_data,
                          measures = measures,
                          pals = pals,
                          labels = fx_ses_labels(map_data)) %>%
    fx_add_rail_layers(rail_lines, rail_stations, station_labels,
                       color = "#808080",
                       radius = 4,
                       fillColor = "#fff") %>%
    addLayersControl(
      overlayGroups = c("L Lines", "L Stations"),
      options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE, position = "topright"))
}
```

## Ridership by community indicator quintile
Next, examine how ridership has changed over time across the quintile categories (Lowest, Low, Moderate, High and Highest) of the indicator you selected. Edit the two lines marked `EDIT HERE` in the code below with your indicator's name and column (from the table above). @fig-ridershipbyses plots weekday boardings at stations in each quintile category of their community area, and @tbl-ridershipbyses summarizes community areas, population, L stations and the change in weekday boardings by quintile category. *In slide 6 of your presentation, paste the plot and table and describe how ridership trends differ across quintile categories. Which categories accounted for the most boardings before the pandemic? Did ridership fall more steeply, or recover more quickly, in less advantaged communities? Using the table, compare each category's share of the city's population with its share of L stations and boardings. What do the differences suggest about who relies on the L, and about equitable access to rail transit [@litman2014]?*

```{r}
#| label: define indicator quintile plotting functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the indicator quintile plotting functions"

# quintile category colors, from Highest to Lowest (as in Exercise #2)
quintile_colors <- c(Highest = "darkred",
                     High = "orange",
                     Moderate = "yellow",
                     Low = "lightblue",
                     Lowest = "darkblue")

# function for adding the selected indicator's values (ses_value) and quintile
# categories (ses_ntile) to community areas
fx_add_ses_quintiles <- function(community_areas_ses, ses_column) {
  quintile_labels <- c("Lowest", "Low", "Moderate", "High", "Highest")
  community_areas_ses %>%
    mutate(ses_value = .data[[ses_column]],
           ses_ntile = factor(quintile_labels[ntile(ses_value, 5)],
                              levels = names(quintile_colors)))
}

# function for plotting weekday boardings by month and quintile category of the
# selected indicator in each station's community area; ses_name labels the legend
fx_plot_ridership_by_ses <- function(rail_stations_ridership, community_areas_ses, ses_name = "Indicator") {
  ridership_by_ses <- rail_stations_ridership %>%
    left_join(community_areas_ses %>%
                st_drop_geometry() %>%
                select(comarea_id, ses_ntile),
              by = "comarea_id") %>%
    drop_na(ses_ntile) %>%
    group_by(year_month, ses_ntile) %>%
    summarise(rides_total = sum(rides_total), .groups = "drop")

  plot_ly(data = ridership_by_ses,
          x = ~year_month,
          y = ~rides_total,
          type = 'scatter',
          mode = 'lines',
          color = ~ses_ntile,
          colors = quintile_colors,
          text = ~ses_ntile,
          hovertemplate = '%{text}: %{y:,}<extra></extra>') %>%
    fx_plot_layout(y_title = "Total Weekday Rail Station Boardings",
                   filename = paste0("cta_rail_boardings_by_", tolower(gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", ses_name)), "_quintile")) %>%
    layout(legend = list(title = list(text = paste0(ses_name, " Quintile  "))))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: define quintile summary table functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the quintile summary table functions"

# function for summarizing community areas, population, L stations and the change
# in weekday boardings by quintile category of the selected indicator, from Highest
# to Lowest, along with each category's share of the city's population, stations
# and latest boardings; stations without boardings in both months are left out
fx_summarise_ses_quintiles <- function(station_change, community_areas_ses) {
  stations <- station_change %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    left_join(community_areas_ses %>%
                st_drop_geometry() %>%
                select(comarea_id, ses_ntile),
              by = "comarea_id") %>%
    group_by(ses_ntile) %>%
    summarise(stations = n(),
              rides_from = sum(rides_from),
              rides_to = sum(rides_to),
              .groups = "drop")

  community_areas_ses %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(ses_ntile) %>%
    summarise(communityareas = n(),
              population = sum(population, na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    left_join(stations, by = "ses_ntile") %>%
    mutate(across(c(stations, rides_from, rides_to), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)),
           pct_chg = (rides_to - rides_from) / rides_from) %>%
    drop_na(ses_ntile) %>%
    mutate(population_pct = population / sum(population),
           stations_pct = stations / sum(stations),
           rides_to_pct = rides_to / sum(rides_to),
           month_from = station_change$month_from[1],
           month_to = station_change$month_to[1]) %>%
    arrange(ses_ntile)
}

# function for formatting the quintile summary as an interactive table; ses_name
# labels the quintile column
fx_table_ses_quintiles <- function(ridership_by_ses_quintile, ses_name = "Indicator") {
  month_from <- format(ridership_by_ses_quintile$month_from[1], "%b %Y")
  month_to <- format(ridership_by_ses_quintile$month_to[1], "%b %Y")
  ridership_by_ses_quintile %>%
    select(-month_from, -month_to) %>%
    datatable(class = 'cell-border stripe',
              selection = "none",
              rownames = FALSE,
              colnames = c(paste(ses_name, "Quintile"), "Community Areas", "Population", "L Stations",
                           paste(month_from, "Weekday Boardings"), paste(month_to, "Weekday Boardings"),
                           "Percent Change", "Percent of Population", "Percent of L Stations",
                           paste("Percent of", month_to, "Weekday Boardings")),
              options = list(searching = FALSE,
                             lengthChange = FALSE,
                             paging = FALSE)) %>%
    formatPercentage(c("pct_chg", "population_pct", "stations_pct", "rides_to_pct"), digits = 1) %>%
    formatRound(c("population", "rides_from", "rides_to"), mark = ",", digits = 0)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ridershipbyses
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("Community Areas, Population, L Stations and Change in Weekday Boardings (", format(ridership_through, "%B"), " 2019-", format(ridership_through, "%Y"), ") by Quintile Category of the Selected Community Indicator")

# calculate the change in weekday boardings by station for all lines, between
# the latest month and the same month in 2019
station_change_all <- fx_station_change(ridership_attributes, rail_stations)

# summarize stations and the change in weekday boardings by quintile category
ridership_by_ses_quintile <- fx_summarise_ses_quintiles(station_change_all, community_areas_ses_q)
fx_table_ses_quintiles(ridership_by_ses_quintile, ses_name)

```

# Step 4. Strategies for improving ridership
In the final step you will act as a transit planner. Drawing on what you learned in Steps 2 and 3 and on this week's required reading, Jarrett Walker's *Human Transit* (chapters 1 and 2) [@walker2012], you will identify parts of the city where L ridership could be improved and propose strategies to do so. There is no single correct answer. What matters is that your proposals are grounded in the evidence and connected to why people do, or do not, choose transit.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Key ideas from *Human Transit*
Walker argues that transit is useful only when it meets the needs of the people who could ride it. He describes **seven demands** that riders place on transit: it takes me where I want to go; it takes me when I want to go; it is a good use of my time; it is a good use of my money; it respects me; I can trust it; and it gives me freedom to change my plans. He also breaks every transit trip into **seven phases**: understanding the service, accessing the stop or station, waiting, paying, riding, connecting and accessing the final destination. Frequency appears in several of these phases, which is why Walker places so much weight on it. Each phase is a place where a trip can become slow, costly, uncomfortable or unreliable enough that a traveler chooses another mode, or chooses not to travel at all.
:::

## Identify focus community areas
@tbl-communityareas lists every community area with at least one L station, along with its number of stations, the change in weekday boardings at those stations and its community indicators. Click a column name to sort the table, or type in the boxes below the column names to filter it (e.g., to show only community areas with a poverty rate in a given range). Community areas without L stations are not listed; use the map in @fig-mapses to find them. Use the table together with the map to choose **three focus community areas**:

1. a community area with less advantaged conditions where ridership has recovered slowly;
2. a community area where ridership has recovered strongly, which may offer lessons for others; and
3. a community area with few or no L stations, where residents may have limited access to rail transit.

*In slide 7 of your presentation, paste a screenshot of the map in @fig-mapses zoomed in to your focus community areas, and describe each one. What do the indicators, station locations and changes in ridership tell you about each community area? Why did you choose it?*

```{r}
#| label: define community area summary table functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the community area summary table functions"

# function for summarizing L stations and the change in weekday boardings by
# community area, along with every community indicator; community areas without
# L stations (with boardings in both months) are left out
fx_summarise_communityareas <- function(station_change, community_areas_ses, indicators = ses_indicators) {
  stations <- station_change %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(comarea_id) %>%
    summarise(stations = n(),
              rides_from = sum(rides_from),
              rides_to = sum(rides_to),
              .groups = "drop")

  community_areas_ses %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(comarea_id, comarea_name, all_of(indicators$column)) %>%
    inner_join(stations, by = "comarea_id") %>%
    mutate(pct_chg = (rides_to - rides_from) / rides_from,
           month_from = station_change$month_from[1],
           month_to = station_change$month_to[1]) %>%
    arrange(comarea_name)
}

# function for formatting the community area summary as an interactive table that
# can be sorted (click a column name) and filtered (boxes under the column names)
fx_table_communityareas <- function(ridership_by_communityarea, indicators = ses_indicators) {
  month_from <- format(ridership_by_communityarea$month_from[1], "%b %Y")
  month_to <- format(ridership_by_communityarea$month_to[1], "%b %Y")
  ridership_by_communityarea %>%
    select(comarea_name, stations, rides_from, rides_to, pct_chg, all_of(indicators$column)) %>%
    datatable(class = 'cell-border stripe',
              selection = "none",
              rownames = FALSE,
              filter = "top",
              colnames = c("Community Area", "L Stations",
                           paste(month_from, "Weekday Boardings"), paste(month_to, "Weekday Boardings"),
                           "Percent Change", indicators$name),
              options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
    formatPercentage("pct_chg", digits = 1) %>%
    formatRound(c("rides_from", "rides_to", "population"), mark = ",", digits = 0) %>%
    formatRound(setdiff(indicators$column, "population"), digits = 1)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-communityareas
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("L Stations, Change in Weekday Boardings (", format(ridership_through, "%B"), " 2019-", format(ridership_through, "%Y"), ") and Community Indicators by Community Area")

# summarize stations, the change in weekday boardings and indicators by community area
ridership_by_communityarea <- fx_summarise_communityareas(station_change_all, community_areas_ses)
fx_table_communityareas(ridership_by_communityarea)

```

## Diagnose barriers and propose strategies
For each focus community area, use Walker's seven demands and seven phases of a trip to diagnose the most important barriers to riding the L, then propose one or two strategies to address them. Think about the whole trip, not just the train ride, and about who lives in and travels to each community area. Strategies might address, for example:

- **Frequency and span:** more frequent service, or service that runs earlier and later, so riders can travel when they want to without consulting a schedule.
- **Speed and reliability:** bus priority lanes and signal priority on routes that feed L stations, or track and signal repairs that remove slow zones.
- **Connections:** bus routes and timed transfers that link neighborhoods without stations to the L, or better connections between lines.
- **Station access:** safer sidewalks and crossings, lighting, bike parking and Divvy stations (Exercise #2) that extend the walkable area around each station.
- **Stations and the riding experience:** safety, cleanliness, accessibility (e.g., elevators) and clear information, all part of whether transit "respects" its riders.
- **Fares:** reduced fares, fare capping or integrated fares that make transit a good use of riders' money.
- **Land use:** housing, jobs and services near stations (transit-oriented development) that put more destinations within reach of the L, while guarding against the displacement of current residents.

As you weigh your proposals, consider their costs and tradeoffs. Resources spent on frequent service in busy corridors can attract the most riders, while resources spent covering every neighborhood ensure access for those who depend on transit most. Consider also how your proposals would affect the benefits of transit for different groups of residents [@toddlitman2017; @litman2014].

*In slide 8 of your presentation, complete the strategy table for your three focus community areas, naming the barrier (by Walker's demand or trip phase), your proposed strategy and its expected effect and tradeoffs. Then propose one citywide strategy that you believe would do the most to increase L ridership in Chicago as a whole. Why did you choose it, who would benefit most, and what would it take to implement?*
